questions.question: How do supply/demand elasticity, cultural negotiation styles, reputation modifiers, and BATNA create a dynamic bargaining economy where player negotiation skill directly impacts purchasing power?
questions.answer: Each NPC has a reservation price determined by supply/demand and faction culture (Keepers: relational bargaining with gifts; Traders: hard numbers). Reputation modifies the band: +10 rep = 5% better rates. BATNA matters — if the NPC has another buyer, prices are less negotiable. A skilled negotiator reading cultural cues and bundling items achieves 20-35% better prices than a click-to-buy player.

questions.question: Does trading with NPCs tell the story of an economy that reflects local conditions — rare here is common there, prices reveal scarcity, and every trade teaches something about supply and demand in a real system?
questions.answer: Trade tells the story of a functional economy: a high price for water in the desert tells you about drought, cheap minerals near the canyon tell you about abundance — the player learns planetary economics through every transaction.

questions.question: Is the trade interface intuitive -- can the player compare item values, adjust offer quantities, and see reputation-based price modifiers without opening nested sub-menus?
questions.answer: Trade screen shows side-by-side inventories with RMB-to-compare tooltip. Quantity uses +/- buttons with instant price recalculation. Reputation modifier is shown as a percentage badge on the trader's portrait. No nested menus.

questions.question: Do trade inventories, prices, supply/demand modifiers, and player reputation per NPC need to persist?
questions.answer: Yes. Each NPC trader has inventory (item IDs + quantities), price modifiers, and dynamically adjusted supply/demand based on recent trades. Written on trade completion or manual save. Write frequency: every trade transaction.

questions.question: Does the trade system model any physical constraints (cargo mass, storage volume, fuel cost of transporting goods) or is it purely economic?
questions.answer: Not in v1. Trade is purely economic (currency-for-goods) with no physical cargo simulation. Cargo mass/volume and transport costs are identified as a future enhancement for the economic system.
